characters.name: The Lunch Angel — The Stranger
characters.description:
The man at the heart of the story. He approaches the Giving Machines on a winter night, hears about the lunch program, walks away, and comes back with a $20 bill and the line that titles our film: "Let's get two, then. Somebody did this for me."

Mid-40s to late 40s. Lean build, slightly hunched against the cold. Dark hair flecked with grey at the temples, slightly long and uneven — like he hasn't seen a barber in some time. Short untrimmed dark beard, a few weeks of growth. Weathered face with high cheekbones. Warm intelligent hazel eyes — there is dignity and gentleness there. He looks like someone who used to have a different life.

Wardrobe: heavy dark olive winter coat worn at the cuffs and collar. Faded red-and-brown plaid flannel shirt visible at the collar with a thermal henley underneath. Grey wool knit beanie pulled low. Dark, well-worn jeans. Heavy work boots, scuffed but solid. He carries a small canvas messenger bag or rolled bedroll over one shoulder — never a trash bag.

POSTURE: Stands with hands deep in coat pockets. Shoulders forward against the cold. Moves carefully, deliberately — a man used to being watched and judged.

DIGNITY NOTE: He should NEVER look pitiful, dirty, or theatrical. He looks like someone's brother who had a hard year. Render him with the same warmth and care as the volunteer. The audience should feel kinship, not pity. That is the entire ethical foundation of this film.
characters.chatgpt_prompt:
I am attaching reference images. The new image must look IDENTICAL in style, technique, and rendering to these references. Match them exactly.

Specifically replicate from the references:
- The HEAVY paper grain texture covering the entire frame including faces and clothing — strong, visible, noisy texture, NOT subtle
- The flat-wash painting style — peach/cream skin tone with one warmer cheek blush, NO skin detail, NO texture, NO pores, NO wrinkles drawn in
- Beards rendered as a single soft cream/grey wash shape, NOT individual hairs
- Eyes drawn as simple dark dots with a small catchlight, NOT detailed irises or eyelid anatomy
- Soft, low-detail face that reads as a STORYBOOK CHARACTER painted in 3-4 flat color washes
- The same dense, scattered painterly snow particles as the references — bright cream dots all over the frame, including across the figure
- The same softly bleeding paper edges (slightly torn / vignette around the frame border)
- The same lavender-purple background tone behind the figure
- Same warm amber lamppost glow

DO NOT produce:
- Any photographic skin detail
- Detailed eye anatomy (irises, eyelid creases, tear ducts)
- Individually rendered beard or eyebrow hairs
- Visible facial wrinkles drawn in detail
- Polished portrait-painting finish
- Smooth digital surfaces

The references show a SOFT, LOW-DETAIL CHILDREN'S BOOK ILLUSTRATION style. The output must match that exact level of simplification. Less detail, not more.

NEW IMAGE TO CREATE:
A storybook illustration of a man in his mid-40s, off-center on the right side of the frame with a snowy Christmas village softly visible on the left.

Character details (rendered with the same softness as the references):
- Mid-40s, lean build
- Hair flecked with grey at the temples — rendered as soft simple shapes, NOT strands
- Short dark beard rendered as a simple cream/grey/brown wash shape, NO individual hair detail
- Soft, simplified facial features — flat peach/cream skin with one warm cheek blush, NO wrinkles drawn in, NO skin texture
- Eyes as simple dark dots with small catchlights, NOT detailed eye anatomy
- Gentle, dignified expression
- Grey wool knit beanie pulled low (like a soft simple shape, no knit detail rendered photographically)
- Heavy dark olive winter coat
- Faded red-and-brown plaid flannel shirt visible at the collar
- Breath faintly visible in the cold air

Background: snowy Christmas village softly out of focus on the left side of the frame, warm amber festival lights as bokeh, gentle painterly falling snow scattered across the entire frame including the figure.

Composition: 3:2 LANDSCAPE orientation. Figure occupies the right 40-50% of the frame, head and shoulders. Village atmosphere fills the left half. Heavy paper grain texture covering everything.

CRITICAL: Match the reference images' simplification level EXACTLY. Less detail, softer, lighter.
characters.notes:
🎯 THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CHARACTER IN THE FILM.

Generate 6-8 variations and choose carefully. The right Lunch Angel:
- Mid-40s (not older — a younger man makes his condition feel situational, not destined)
- Hazel eyes that read as intelligent and warm
- Beard that's a few weeks unkempt (not months — not theatrical)
- Beanie, not flat cap (so he's visually distinct from Doug at every distance)
- No facial scars, no obvious illness, no theatrical grime

REJECT versions that:
- Make him look pitiable or wretched
- Suggest illness or injury
- Use cliched homeless visual stereotypes (sign, shopping cart, etc.)
- Read as too clean or staged

The boy in the flashback (Shot 20) should subtly echo this character's coloring — same warm hazel eyes, similar bone structure. Don't tell the audience they're connected. Let them feel it.

Brown hair (soft wash), dark warm-brown eyes (small cartoon dot-eyes with one tiny bright catchlight — NO realistic iris detail), peach skin with one round soft cheek blush per side, eyebrows as small confident ink strokes, mouth as a single small soft curve. Real-proportioned 8-year-old body — kid-sized but realistic shape, not chibi. Wearing a slightly oversized hoodie or sweatshirt over a plain t-shirt and jeans. EXPRESSION CRITICAL: Quiet, patient, careful. NOT sad. NOT crying. NOT pitiful. He is a child who has been told what to do and is doing it — the kind of patient that doesn't belong on an 8-year-old. The viewer should want to protect him, not pity him. Generate 4 variations: quiet/waiting, small careful smile, looking down, surprised/relieved (for the moment the tray arrives).

DO NOT: realistic eye anatomy, painted iris, photographic skin texture, anything that reads 'photoreal child'. He is the cartoon-faced kid we love and need to protect.
